answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: From FDR’s First Inaugural Address, delivered at the U.S. Capitol on 4 March 1933 at the depth of the Great Depression. His actual words were “Happiness lies not in the mere possession of money; it lies in the joy of achievement, in the thrill of creative effort” — confirmed in Yale’s Avalon Project ↗ and the American Presidency Project ↗.

source.excerpt: The measure of the restoration lies in the extent to which we apply social values more noble than mere monetary profit. Happiness lies not in the mere possession of money; it lies in the joy of achievement, in the thrill of creative effort. The joy and moral stimulation of work no longer must be forgotten in the mad chase of evanescent profits.
trail: The address as delivered on 4 March 1933 is preserved in full by Yale’s Avalon Project ↗, which carries the sentence verbatim.
The American Presidency Project ↗ at UC Santa Barbara reproduces the identical wording.
Wikisource ↗ hosts the public-domain transcript, confirming the line word for word.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version keeps only the middle clause — dropping “not in the mere possession of money” and swapping the second “in” for “and”
source.excerptNote: The famous condensed form — “Happiness lies in the joy of achievement and the thrill of creative effort” — is an accurate attribution to FDR but an inexact quotation. It strips out the anti-materialist contrast that gave the line its meaning in 1933.

author.heading: About Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.bio: Franklin Delano Roosevelt (1882–1945) was the 32nd President of the United States, elected to four terms and serving from 1933 until his death in 1945. He took office at the depth of the Great Depression, and his First Inaugural Address — best remembered for “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself” — framed the New Deal’s moral case against the unchecked pursuit of profit. The line about happiness comes from that same speech.

misattribution.heading: A misquote, not a misattribution
misattribution.intro: The credit to Franklin D. Roosevelt is correct — but the wording most people share has been trimmed and reworded from what he actually said.

items.who: “Happiness lies in the joy of achievement and the thrill of creative effort”
items.why: This condensed version drops FDR’s opening clause and replaces “in the thrill” with “and the thrill.” His actual sentence in the 1933 inaugural ↗ reads “Happiness lies not in the mere possession of money; it lies in the joy of achievement, in the thrill of creative effort.”

misattribution.truthLine: It is genuinely Roosevelt, from his First Inaugural Address of 4 March 1933 ↗ — just quote the full sentence if you want to quote him accurately.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Roosevelt delivered these words on 4 March 1933, with roughly a quarter of the American workforce unemployed and the banking system in collapse. The passage was not a standalone aphorism about self-fulfillment but part of a pointed argument: that the country’s recovery required valuing work and achievement over “mere monetary profit.”

In its full form — “Happiness lies not in the mere possession of money; it lies in the joy of achievement, in the thrill of creative effort” — the line drives toward his next sentence about “the mad chase of evanescent profits.” The popular short version, stripped of the money clause, reads as a generic motivational slogan and loses that Depression-era edge.
detailsBody: Quote databases such as BrainyQuote, PassItOn, and Goodreads circulate the condensed form, which is why it now appears on posters and social media without the opening clause. The attribution to FDR is nonetheless correct — this is a case of loose quotation, not false authorship.
The exact historical text, preserved in multiple public-domain archives, keeps the contrast Roosevelt intended. Where precision matters, cite the full sentence.
context.pull: He wasn’t praising ambition in the abstract — he was indicting the “mad chase of evanescent profits.”
